analysis.one_liner: Requires the President, Vice President, members of Congress, and candidates to release seven years of tax returns.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2019 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it; it died without a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal tax law so the Treasury Department must publish the tax returns of the President, the Vice President, every member of Congress, and candidates for those offices, covering the previous seven years [S2] [S3]. It would strip out Social Security numbers, financial account numbers, home addresses, and the names of anyone under 18 before release [S3]. The returns would be published within weeks of a candidate entering a race, or by April 30 each year for people already in office [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Voters and the general public, who would be able to see for themselves whether the people who write the tax laws and control the federal purse have financial stakes that conflict with their official duties. Government watchdog groups and journalists would also gain a reliable, standardized record instead of relying on voluntary releases or leaks.

how_it_helps.text: It would have made the tax returns of the President, Vice President, members of Congress, and candidates for those offices a matter of public record, covering the prior seven years [S2] [S3].

Disclosure would be automatic and standardized: candidates' returns published within 15 days of entering a race, and officeholders' returns by April 30 each year, removing the ability of any individual officeholder to simply decline [S3].
The bill carved out sensitive personal details, so the public would see the finances without Social Security numbers, account numbers, minors' names, or home addresses [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The President, Vice President, members of Congress, and candidates would lose financial privacy, with their returns, income sources, and business dealings opened to public and press scrutiny every year. There is no fiscal cost to taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: The President, Vice President, and members of Congress

drawbacks.text: Mandatory annual publication goes far beyond existing financial disclosure: it would expose detailed personal income, deductions, and family business arrangements of every member of Congress each year, including details about spouses and dependents that current ethics forms do not require [S3].

Opponents of return disclosure generally argue that existing annual financial disclosure forms, which members must already file publicly, are sufficient for spotting conflicts of interest; this bill would layer a second, more intrusive regime on top.

Some argue the requirement could deter qualified people with complex finances from running for office at all, though the bill's carve-outs for sensitive personal data were designed to blunt that objection [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a meaningful public check on whether the people writing tax law and managing federal money have personal financial stakes in their own decisions. The cost is real but narrow: sitting officeholders and candidates give up financial privacy, with sensitive details like addresses and children's names already excluded. On balance the public-interest gain outweighs the privacy burden on roughly 540 elected officials, though a poorly regulated release of returns could still expose family members to harassment.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it quietly expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Posey introduced the Tax Transparency Act of 2019 in the House on March 4, 2019 [S1] [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax law [S5].
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both House Democrats [S4].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote. The bill died in committee when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting officeholders are better off: their tax returns remain private, and no law now requires any president, vice president, or member of Congress to disclose them. The public got nothing, since the bill never advanced far enough for anyone to vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call to split by party; its sponsorship was nominally bipartisan, a Republican sponsor with two Democratic cosponsors, but support was minimal from both parties.

industries.industry: Sitting officeholders (President, Vice President, members of Congress) and candidates for those offices
industries.note: The bill would have stripped these officials of financial privacy by publishing seven years of their tax returns annually. They had the power to keep the bill from advancing, and no comparable disclosure exists in law, so their interest in this bill ran directly against the public's interest in seeing their finances.
